Workshop 4 · Sessions 10–12 · Thursday 22 October 2026

Good review or bad review? Bayes' theorem and Naïve Bayes, built by counting

An app shouts "WOLF!" and is right 90% of the time. Should you run? The answer, about 8%, surprises almost everyone, and the reasoning behind it is Bayes' theorem. Today you learn it by counting, then use the same counting to read the feeling of a review, word by word, and test whether your classifier is any good.

Open slides Notebooks and data Practice problems

By the end of this workshop you can

  • work out a Bayes' theorem answer by counting 1000 cases, and name the prior, likelihood, evidence and posterior
  • explain why a rare thing stays unlikely even after a fairly accurate alarm
  • explain the naïve assumption: each word is treated as a separate clue, so we can just multiply
  • train a Naïve Bayes sentiment classifier by hand and in plain Python, with add-one smoothing
  • judge a classifier with accuracy, a confusion table, precision and recall, against a do-nothing baseline

Course outcome CO2 · Reading: [SLP] Appendix B

Before class: pre-read

1. Checklist

  • git pull run in your ADS6703 folder, so the two Workshop 4 notebooks are in ADS6703/w04/

2. Where you already meet sentiment analysis

Sentiment analysis means reading the feeling of a text: is this review, tweet or email positive or negative? Companies run it on everything customers write:

  • a shop flags 1★-sounding reviews so the support team replies first
  • a brand tracks whether posts about its new phone are getting happier or angrier, week by week
  • a bank sorts complaints from thank-you notes before a person reads them

We build one with Naïve Bayes: the same counting and multiplying as in W3, plus one famous rule about probability, Bayes' theorem.

3. The whole idea in five minutes

Bayes' theorem: count, don't guess. An app tells dogs from wolves. Only 10 in 1000 photos are wolves. It catches 90% of wolves, but also calls 10% of dogs a wolf. It shouts "WOLF!": how likely is it really a wolf? Count 1000 photos:

Photos Alarms
Wolves 10 90% of 10 = 9
Dogs 990 10% of 990 = 99
108 alarms in all

Really a wolf = 9 ÷ 108 ≈ 8%, not 90%. Wolves were rare to start with. That starting belief is the prior; the updated one, 8%, is the posterior.

Naïve Bayes: many clues at once. In a review, every word is a small clue. great turns up a lot in positive reviews, broke in negative ones. The classifier:

  1. starts from the prior: how common positive reviews are
  2. multiplies in one probability per word, P(word | pos): how often that word appears in positive reviews
  3. does the same for negative, and picks the bigger score

It pretends each word is a separate clue, which is plainly wrong (not and good belong together). That is the naïve part, and it works surprisingly well.

The zero problem, again. If noisy never appeared in a positive review, its number is 0, and one zero wipes out every other clue. The fix is the one from W3: add-one smoothing.

Is it any good? Test it on reviews it has never seen. If 6 of 10 test reviews are positive, a "classifier" that always says positive already scores 60%. Ours has to beat that, and actually catch the unhappy customers.

4. Read

  • [SLP] Jurafsky & Martin, Appendix B, Naive Bayes, Text Classification, and Sentiment: the sections on the Naive Bayes classifier, training it (including Laplace, that is add-one, smoothing), the worked example, and evaluation (precision, recall). Skip the parts on log probabilities and on F-measure: we don't need them yet.

5. Try (optional)

Pick a product you own and open its reviews on any shopping site. Find one review that a word-counting program would probably get wrong, and work out why: a not, a but, sarcasm, a word with two meanings. Bring it to class.

Handout: Bayes and Naïve Bayes cheat sheet

Print this page, or keep it open during the labs.

Words

prior belief before the clue: P(wolf), P(pos)
likelihood how often the clue appears when A is true: P(alarm | wolf)
evidence how often the clue appears at all: P(alarm)
posterior belief after the clue: P(wolf | alarm)
naïve treat every word as a separate clue
vocabulary, V the different words in the training reviews

Formulas

conditional P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B)
product rule P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) · P(B) = P(B | A) · P(A)
Bayes P(A | B) = P(B | A) · P(A) ÷ P(B)
evidence P(B) = P(B | A) · P(A) + P(B | ¬A) · P(¬A)
word, add-one (count in label + 1) ÷ (words in label + V)
score prior × P(word₁ | label) × P(word₂ | label) × …

Is it any good?

accuracy correct ÷ all
baseline always say the most common label
precision caught ÷ (caught + false alarms)
recall caught ÷ (caught + missed)
test reviews never used for counting

Worked example: six tiny reviews

Positive: great fan · quiet and great · works well   Negative: noisy fan · broke and noisy · fan broke

P(pos) = P(neg) = 3/6. Both piles have 7 words; V = 8, so every add-one fraction has 7 + 8 = 15 at the bottom.

Word Pos count Neg count P(word | pos), add-one P(word | neg), add-one
great 2 0 3/15 1/15
fan 1 2 2/15 3/15
noisy 0 2 1/15 3/15

"great fan but noisy": skip but (never seen). Positive: ½ × 3/15 × 2/15 × 1/15; negative: ½ × 1/15 × 3/15 × 3/15. The tops are 6 and 9, so negative, with 9 ÷ 15 = 60%.

Python

for text, label in train: go through (text, label) pairs
pos_counts.update(text.split()) count the words of a review
set(pos_counts) \| set(neg_counts) the vocabulary
(counts[w] + 1) / (sum(counts.values()) + V) add-one word probability
if word not in vocab: continue skip unknown words
pos / (pos + neg) turn two scores into a probability
